191	Due to the 20min finality buffer, someone can change claim state right before we execute a task. When `challenge`, `start_verification`, or `verify_snapshot` reverts with "Invalid claim" (claimHash mismatch), we reschedule +30min to give the indexer time to catch up and update ClaimStore with fresh claim data.
192	
193	### Race Conditions
194	
195	Each task has its own way of detecting and handling race conditions (another validator did the job first):
196	
197	| Task | Detection | Handling |
198	|------|-----------|----------|
199	| `save_snapshot` | snapshot count unchanged | skip (no-op) |
200	| `claim` | `claimHashes[epoch] != 0` (pre-check) | drop task |
201	| `claim` | `stateRoot` already matches | drop task |
202	| `claim` | state root in pending claim | drop task |
203	| `claim` | on revert: `claimHashes[epoch] != 0` | drop task |
204	| `challenge` | on revert: `Challenged` event emitted | drop task |
205	| `challenge` | on revert: `VerificationStarted` event emitted | reschedule +20min |
206	| `send_snapshot` | (none - cheap, idempotent) | always try |
207	| `start_verification` | `challenger != 0` | drop task |
208	| `start_verification` | on revert: `VerificationStarted` event emitted | drop task |
209	| `start_verification` | on revert: `Challenged` event emitted | drop task |
210	| `verify_snapshot` | `challenger != 0` | drop task |
211	| `verify_snapshot` | on revert: `Verified` event emitted | drop task |
212	| `verify_snapshot` | on revert: `Challenged` event emitted | drop task |
213	| `execute_relay` | `isSpent(position) == true` | drop task |
214	| `execute_relay` | `roots(root) == 0` | reschedule +1hr |
215	| `execute_relay` | any revert | drop task (unreliable error messages from Arbitrum outbox) |
216	| `withdraw_deposit` | `claimHashes[epoch] == 0` (pre-check) | drop task |
217	| `withdraw_deposit` | on revert: `claimHashes[epoch] == 0` | drop task |
218	| any write task | our own transaction mined but not durable (`AwaitingFinality`) | keep task unchanged, re-check next cycle |
219	
220	**Frontrun detection via event checks:** When a task reverts, we check if the expected event was emitted in recent blocks (last 500 blocks, capped at 1000 block range for RPC compatibility). This detects frontruns where another validator's tx landed between our pre-check and tx execution. If the event exists, the job was done - we drop the task. For `challenge`, if `VerificationStarted` was emitted (rare edge case during resync), we reschedule +20min to wait for finality before retrying with updated claim data.
221	
222	### Write durability (reorg-safety of our own writes)
223	
224	Reads are reorg-safe: the indexer ignores anything within 20min of the head. Writes were
225	not. `send_or_replace` used to return as soon as `get_receipt()` resolved - one
226	confirmation - and the dispatcher retires a task the moment its action returns `Ok(())`.
227	A `Challenge` task only ever exists because `validate_claim` created one, and
228	`validate_claim` removes itself the moment it has done so. If the challenge transaction
229	were then reorged out, the `Challenged` event would never be (re-)observed, `SendSnapshot`
230	would never be scheduled, and **nothing would re-examine the claim**: the record keeps
231	`challenger == 0` forever, the deposit is gone, and the fraudulent claim verifies
232	unopposed.
233	
234	So a write is only reported successful once it is durable. `Ok(())` from
235	`send_or_replace` now means "mined, succeeded, and past the bar", not "confirmed".
236	
237	**The bar - `Durability` (`src/tasks/mod.rs`):**
238	
239	| Variant | Means | Used by |
240	|---------|-------|---------|
241	| `Confirmed` | one confirmation, no gate | `claim` only |
242	| `ChainFinalized` | the sending chain's own `finalized` tag has reached the receipt's block | `challenge`, `start_verification`, `verify_snapshot`, `execute_relay` |
243	| `ArbitrumBatchFinalized { l1_provider, sequencer_inbox }` | the receipt's L2 block sits in a sequencer batch whose L1 posting block is finalized | `send_snapshot` |
244	
245	Ethereum and Gnosis both finalize under their own consensus, so their `finalized` tag is
246	exactly "cannot be reorged" and is the right bar for a settlement-chain write.
247	`execute_relay` is on that list because the Arbitrum Outbox it calls lives on L1.
248	
249	`save_snapshot` and `withdraw_deposit` are the two writes that do not go through
250	`send_or_replace` at all, so neither is nonce-pinned or gated: the first is idempotent and
251	costs only L2 gas, and the second moves our own deposit, where a lost write means an
252	uncollected deposit rather than an unopposed fraudulent claim.
253	
254	`claim` is the one exception, and it is an exception because a gate there would protect
255	nothing. Claiming is driven by `EpochWatcher`, and every early return in `claim::execute`
256	- "Already claimed" in particular - happens *before* `send_or_replace` is reached, so once
257	our claim is on chain the function stops at that check and never re-enters the gate to
258	settle the pending record. The record would sit in the store forever, one per epoch,
259	pinning a consumed nonce. And a reorged-out claim costs nothing: the deposit rides on the
260	claim transaction, so undoing the transaction undoes the deposit with it. (It is not
261	re-sent either - `EpochWatcher` records `last_after_epoch` on the first `Ok` - which
262	leaves us exactly where we would have been had we never claimed.)
263	
264	**The sentinel - `AWAITING_FINALITY` (`"AwaitingFinality"`):** returned by
265	`send_or_replace` when the transaction has a receipt that has not cleared the bar. It is
266	distinct from `"PendingReplacement"` on purpose: that one means "still in the mempool,
267	replace it with a higher fee next cycle", this one means "already on chain, replacing it
268	would be a duplicate". `dispatcher.rs` matches it exactly and keeps the task unchanged;
269	`epoch_watcher.rs` and the tasks themselves go through `tasks::is_in_flight`, which covers
270	both sentinels. A task must return an in-flight error untouched rather than falling
271	through to its "did someone else do it?" checks - those read the chain, and for a
272	mined-but-not-durable transaction they would find *our own* effect, read it as a lost race
273	and retire the task, which is the exact hole this closes.
274	
275	**What is stored:** `RouteState.pending_txs` in the route's schedule JSON, keyed
276	`"{action}:{epoch}"`, holding `PendingTx { nonce, max_fee, priority_fee, tx_hash }`. The
277	nonce and fees are written *before* the send, the hash immediately after it, so a crash at
278	any point still leaves the next run able to look the transaction up instead of sending
279	over it. The record is kept for `AwaitingFinality` and cleared only on a terminal outcome
280	(durable success, or a revert that consumed the nonce). Task invalidation and task removal
281	both leave it alone.
282	
283	**Each cycle, for a record that carries a hash:**
284	
285	| Chain's answer | Outcome |
286	|----------------|---------|
287	| receipt, succeeded, durable | clear the record, `Ok(())` - task retires |
288	| receipt, succeeded, not durable | keep the record, `Err(AwaitingFinality)` - task waits |
289	| receipt, reverted | clear the record, normal revert error - the task's post-revert event checks run |
290	| no receipt (never mined, or reorged out) | keep the record and re-send at the **same** nonce, fee-bumped |
291	| RPC error, missing block number, or a failed durability read | treated as not durable - wait |
292	
293	The last row is the direction that matters: an endpoint that will not answer is not
294	evidence that a transaction is absent or final. Waiting another cycle is recoverable;
295	re-sending over a mined write (a second deposit) or retiring a task whose write vanished
296	is not.
297	
298	**`is_l2_block_finalized` (`src/finality.rs`):** the L2 bar, used for `send_snapshot`.
299	Takes the receipt's *own* L2 block, resolves the batch containing it via
300	`NodeInterface.findBatchContainingBlock`, finds the matching
301	`SequencerInbox.SequencerBatchDelivered` on L1 by paginated log scan, and compares that L1
302	block against L1's `finalized` tag - the same method `is_epoch_finalized` uses, sharing its
303	tail. It exists separately because "the epoch is finalized" is not the statement we need:
304	a transaction sent after epoch end sits in a later L2 block and therefore a later batch,
305	which may not have been posted to L1 at all when the epoch-end batch already has. Gating on
306	`is_epoch_finalized` would report durable while the write itself was still only
307	sequencer-promised.
308	
309	The L1 log scan starts one hour (`BATCH_SCAN_SKEW_SECS`) *before* the L2 block's own
310	timestamp. Arbitrum derives L2 timestamps from the sequencer's view of L1 time and lets
311	them run ahead of it, so the raw timestamp can resolve to an L1 block after the batch was
312	posted, and a forward-only scan started there would walk past the event and report "not
313	finalized" permanently. An hour is well clear of the protocol's future-time bound and costs
314	at most ~300 L1 blocks, a fraction of the first 2000-block page.
315	
316	Like `is_epoch_finalized`, it returns `Ok(true)` immediately when `sequencer_inbox` is
317	`None` - that is how the Anvil devnet, which has no rollup, runs; `startup.rs` panics if it
318	is unset in production. Every other unknown ("the node does not have that block yet", "no
319	batch event within the scan cap") is reported as *not* finalized, so the caller waits.
320	
321	**Not covered:** a *third party's* challenge that is reorged out after we indexed it - we
322	would keep a claim record naming a challenger the chain no longer has, and the claim-hash
323	invariant turns that into a reverted transaction rather than a wrong verdict. A `Verified`
324	that is reorged out is likewise out of scope: that event is only accepted by the indexer
325	once it is more than 20 minutes old.
326	
327	### Missing Claim Data
328	
329	If we see `Verified`, `VerificationStarted`, or `Challenged` for an epoch whose `Claimed` event was emitted before our sync window, we drop it - we can't reconstruct claim data we never saw.
330	
331	**Starting mid-bridge:** The validator can be started at any time. On first run (or after a hiatus longer than `sync_lookback_secs`), `indexing_since` is set to `now - sync_lookback_secs` and persisted. Events for epochs whose `Claimed` was before this window are dropped - the contract only stores a claim hash, so the full `Claim` struct can only be reconstructed from witnessing the original `Claimed` event.
332	
333	## SnapshotSent Filtering
334	
335	The indexer only processes `SnapshotSent` events from transactions it sent itself (checked via `tx.signer == wallet_address`).
336	
337	**Why?** `sendSnapshot()` is cheap to call with arbitrary data. An attacker could spam bogus snapshots with invalid `Claim` parameters. If we processed all `SnapshotSent` events, we'd waste gas relaying L2→L1 messages that would revert on Arbitrum's outbox (wrong proof/claim data).
338	
339	**How it works:** When the validator sees a `Challenged` event, it calls `sendSnapshot` itself. By only indexing our own `SnapshotSent` events, we guarantee we're relaying messages we know are correct.
340	
341	**Alternative approach (not implemented):** Parse the `L2ToL1Tx` calldata, compare the embedded `Claim` against our `ClaimStore`, verify no prior `SnapshotSent` exists for that epoch, then schedule the relay. This would let us piggyback on other validators' snapshots but adds complexity. The `isSpent` check in `execute_relay` would then serve as the final guard against duplicate relays. For v1, self-filtering is simpler and sufficient.
342	
343	## Route-Specific Logic
344	
345	Two types of route-specific branching:
346	
347	**Deposit logic** (`weth_address.is_some()`): Used when the difference is ETH vs WETH deposits.
348	
349	| Task | WETH route | ETH route |
350	|------|------------|-----------|
351	| `claim` | no `.value(deposit)` | `.value(deposit)` |
352	| `challenge` | check WETH balance, no `.value(deposit)` | check ETH balance, `.value(deposit)` |
353	
354	**Contract signatures** (`match route.name`): Used when contracts have different function signatures.
355	
356	| Task | ARB_TO_ETH | ARB_TO_GNOSIS |
357	|------|------------|---------------|
358	| `send_snapshot` | `sendSnapshot(epoch, claim)` | `sendSnapshot(epoch, gas_limit, claim)` |
359	
360	## L2 Finality Verification
361	
362	Before executing critical tasks (`validate_claim`, `claim`, `challenge`), the validator verifies the epoch's L2 data is finalized on L1. This prevents acting on data that could theoretically be reorged.
363	
364	**How it works:**
365	1. Convert epoch → end timestamp: `(epoch + 1) * epoch_period`
366	2. Binary search to find the L2 block at that timestamp
367	3. Query `NodeInterface.findBatchContainingBlock(l2_block)` on Arbitrum to get the batch number
368	4. Search for `SequencerInbox.SequencerBatchDelivered(batchNum)` event on L1 to find which L1 block contains the batch
369	5. Compare that L1 block against `eth_getBlockByNumber("finalized")` - if finalized block >= batch block, the epoch is finalized
370	
371	**Batch event query strategy:** Batches are posted to L1 after L2 transactions, but timing varies significantly - mainnet posts every ~1-3 minutes, while testnet can have gaps of hours or days. To find the `SequencerBatchDelivered` event reliably:
372	1. Binary search L1 to find the block at `epoch_end_ts` (batch must be posted after the L2 block exists)
373	2. Paginate forward in 2000-block chunks (~6.6 hours each) until we find the event or reach L1's latest block
374	3. If not found after scanning to latest, return "not finalized" and reschedule the task for +30 minutes
375	
376	This approach handles arbitrary batch posting delays without hitting RPC block range limits. If the paginated search becomes too slow in production, we'll switch to indexing `SequencerBatchDelivered` events.
377	
378	**Configuration:**
379	- `SEQUENCER_INBOX`: Address of Arbitrum's SequencerInbox on Ethereum L1. **Required in production** - `startup.rs` panics if not set.
380	- For tests (local Anvil chains), `SEQUENCER_INBOX` is not set. When `sequencer_inbox` is `None`, finality checks return `Ok(true)` immediately, bypassing the check.
381	
382	**Why finality matters:**
383	- The 20-minute buffer after epoch end is a heuristic, not a guarantee
384	- Real finality depends on batch posting to L1 and L1 block finalization (~15-20 min on mainnet)
385	- Without finality checks, a validator could challenge a valid claim if L2 data reorged after they read it
386	
387	**Task behavior when not finalized:**
388	- `ValidateClaim` returns `Err("EpochNotFinalized")` and gets rescheduled +30 minutes.
389	  The finality check and the snapshot read live together in
390	  `validate_claim::finalized_state_root`, which is the single entry point for any verdict.
391	- `Claim` (epoch watcher): returns `Err("EpochNotFinalized")`, retries after 5 minutes. If someone else claims in the meantime, the "Already claimed" check in `claim::execute` detects it and stops.
392	- This is expected during normal operation when tasks are scheduled close to epoch boundaries, or on testnet where batch posting is sporadic
393

398	L2→L1 message relay requires the merkle root to be confirmed on the L1 Arbitrum Outbox before `executeTransaction` can succeed. Roots are posted when rollup assertions are confirmed (after `confirmPeriodBlocks`). If the root isn't confirmed yet, `execute_relay` detects this via `outbox.roots(root) == 0` and reschedules +1 hour.

## Project context

### `DESIGN_AND_RATIONALE.md` (verbatim at lane HEAD)

# VEA Validator Design & Rationale

Rust validator for the VEA (Verified Ethereum Attestation) bridge. Monitors claims, challenges fraud, and relays messages between Arbitrum and destination chains (Ethereum, Gnosis).

## Architecture

```
main.rs
  ├── startup checks (RPC health, balances, WETH approval)
  └── per route:
        ├── EpochWatcher  - tracks epoch timing, saves snapshots at epoch end, optionally makes claims
        ├── EventIndexer  - scans inbox/outbox events, schedules tasks
        └── TaskDispatcher - executes scheduled tasks
```

## Routes

- `ARB_TO_ETH`: Arbitrum → Ethereum (native ETH deposits)
- `ARB_TO_GNOSIS`: Arbitrum → Gnosis (WETH deposits)

## Core Components

### EpochWatcher
Polls every 10s. Two responsibilities:
1. **Save snapshot** ~60s before epoch ends (if messages exist and count changed)
2. **Make claim** ~20min after epoch starts (if `MAKE_CLAIMS=true` and synced)

**Snapshot saving logic:** The indexer tracks `last_saved_count` from `SnapshotSaved` events. Before saving, we compare `inbox.count()` to `last_saved_count`:
- If `count == 0`: no messages, skip
- If `count <= last_saved_count`: nothing new, skip
- If `last_saved_count` is unknown (None): treat as 0, save if messages exist

**Cold-start behavior:** If no `SnapshotSaved` events exist in the sync window (fresh chain or long hiatus), `last_saved_count` defaults to 0. This ensures the validator will save a snapshot if any messages exist, preventing bridge staleness when this is the only validator running.

**20min buffer edge case:** Since `SnapshotSaved` events are processed with the same 20min finality buffer as other events, if another validator saves a snapshot within the last 20min of an epoch, this validator won't see it yet and may call `saveSnapshot()` redundantly. This is acceptable, since L2 gas is cheap.

**Why claims are optional:** To challenge fraud, the validator needs ETH/WETH for deposits. Making claims locks funds on the outbox. During an attack, a conservative validator should preserve capital for challenges rather than tie it up in claims.

### EventIndexer
Scans inbox/outbox logs in chunks. Only processes events from blocks older than 20min (finality buffer).

Reacts to events:
- `outbox.Claimed` → schedules `task::validate_claim`
  - if valid → schedules `task::start_verification` (after `start_verification_delay`)
  - if invalid → schedules `task::challenge`
- `outbox.VerificationStarted` → schedules `task::verify_snapshot` (after minChallengePeriod)
- `outbox.Challenged` → schedules `task::send_snapshot`
- `outbox.Verified` → schedules `task::withdraw_deposit`
- `inbox.SnapshotSent` → schedules `task::execute_relay` (after `relay_delay`), **only if emitted by this validator**
- `inbox.SnapshotSaved` → updates `last_saved_count` (used by save_snapshot logic)

### TaskDispatcher
Polls every 15s. Executes tasks when `execute_after` timestamp reached.

### TaskStore / ClaimStore
Each route has its own JSON files for persistence:
- **TaskStore**: scheduled tasks, indexer block cursors, `indexing_since` timestamp, `on_sync` flag
- **ClaimStore**: claim data (state root, claimer, timestamps, challenger, honest party) needed to reconstruct `Claim` structs for contract calls

## Task Types

| Task | Trigger | Action |
|------|---------|--------|
| `save_snapshot` | epoch end | calls `inbox.saveSnapshot()` |
| `claim` | epoch start | claims epoch on outbox |
| `validate_claim` | Claimed event | compares state roots, schedules challenge or start_verification |
| `challenge` | invalid claim | challenges with deposit |
| `send_snapshot` | Challenged event | sends snapshot via native bridge |
| `start_verification` | valid claim (after `start_verification_delay`) | starts verification period |
| `verify_snapshot` | VerificationStarted + minChallengePeriod | finalizes verification |
| `execute_relay` | SnapshotSent (after `relay_delay`) | executes L2→L1 message on Arbitrum Outbox |
| `withdraw_deposit` | Verified event | withdraws to honest party |

## Sync Behavior

On startup, indexer initializes from `now - sync_lookback_secs`. The lookback is computed dynamically from contract parameters: `relay_delay + start_verification_delay + min_challenge_period + buffer`. Events older than sync window are dropped gracefully. Tasks only execute when `on_sync=true`.

## Error Handling

### RPC Resilience
- **30s HTTP timeout** on all RPC providers (10s connect timeout) — prevents infinite hangs on unresponsive endpoints
- **Binary search (`find_block_by_timestamp`)**: retries each individual RPC call 3x with exponential backoff (5s, 15s, 45s) before panicking. Binary search state (lo/hi) preserved between retries.
- **Indexer `scan_chain`**: returns false on RPC failure, retries next cycle (1s later). Does not crash the route.
- **Epoch watcher**: logs warning and continues loop on RPC failure. Claim RPC timeouts/connection errors are also handled gracefully (warn + retry next cycle). Non-RPC claim errors still panic.
- **Task dispatcher**: logs warning and returns early on RPC failure (retries next cycle, 15s later). Does not crash the route.
- **Fallback layer**: with multiple RPCs configured, failures rotate to the next RPC automatically

### General Errors
- **RPC failures during indexing**: logged, retry next poll
- **Task failures**: task stays in queue, retried next poll
- **`Insufficient funds` on Challenge**: rescheduled +30min
- **`Invalid claim` reverts**: rescheduled +30min (see below)
- **`AwaitingFinality`**: the task's transaction is mined but not durable yet. The task is

### Write durability (reorg-safety of our own writes)

Reads are reorg-safe: the indexer ignores anything within 20min of the head. Writes were
not. `send_or_replace` used to return as soon as `get_receipt()` resolved - one
confirmation - and the dispatcher retires a task the moment its action returns `Ok(())`.
A `Challenge` task only ever exists because `validate_claim` created one, and
`validate_claim` removes itself the moment it has done so. If the challenge transaction
were then reorged out, the `Challenged` event would never be (re-)observed, `SendSnapshot`
would never be scheduled, and **nothing would re-examine the claim**: the record keeps
`challenger == 0` forever, the deposit is gone, and the fraudulent claim verifies
unopposed.

So a write is only reported successful once it is durable. `Ok(())` from
`send_or_replace` now means "mined, succeeded, and past the bar", not "confirmed".

**The bar - `Durability` (`src/tasks/mod.rs`):**

| Variant | Means | Used by |
|---------|-------|---------|
| `Confirmed` | one confirmation, no gate | `claim` only |
| `ChainFinalized` | the sending chain's own `finalized` tag has reached the receipt's block | `challenge`, `start_verification`, `verify_snapshot`, `execute_relay` |
| `ArbitrumBatchFinalized { l1_provider, sequencer_inbox }` | the receipt's L2 block sits in a sequencer batch whose L1 posting block is finalized | `send_snapshot` |

Ethereum and Gnosis both finalize under their own consensus, so their `finalized` tag is
exactly "cannot be reorged" and is the right bar for a settlement-chain write.
`execute_relay` is on that list because the Arbitrum Outbox it calls lives on L1.

`save_snapshot` and `withdraw_deposit` are the two writes that do not go through
`send_or_replace` at all, so neither is nonce-pinned or gated: the first is idempotent and
costs only L2 gas, and the second moves our own deposit, where a lost write means an
uncollected deposit rather than an unopposed fraudulent claim.

`claim` is the one exception, and it is an exception because a gate there would protect
nothing. Claiming is driven by `EpochWatcher`, and every early return in `claim::execute`
- "Already claimed" in particular - happens *before* `send_or_replace` is reached, so once
our claim is on chain the function stops at that check and never re-enters the gate to
settle the pending record. The record would sit in the store forever, one per epoch,
pinning a consumed nonce. And a reorged-out claim costs nothing: the deposit rides on the
claim transaction, so undoing the transaction undoes the deposit with it. (It is not
re-sent either - `EpochWatcher` records `last_after_epoch` on the first `Ok` - which
leaves us exactly where we would have been had we never claimed.)

**The sentinel - `AWAITING_FINALITY` (`"AwaitingFinality"`):** returned by
`send_or_replace` when the transaction has a receipt that has not cleared the bar. It is
distinct from `"PendingReplacement"` on purpose: that one means "still in the mempool,
replace it with a higher fee next cycle", this one means "already on chain, replacing it
would be a duplicate". `dispatcher.rs` matches it exactly and keeps the task unchanged;
`epoch_watcher.rs` and the tasks themselves go through `tasks::is_in_flight`, which covers
both sentinels. A task must return an in-flight error untouched rather than falling
through to its "did someone else do it?" checks - those read the chain, and for a
mined-but-not-durable transaction they would find *our own* effect, read it as a lost race
and retire the task, which is the exact hole this closes.

**What is stored:** `RouteState.pending_txs` in the route's schedule JSON, keyed
`"{action}:{epoch}"`, holding `PendingTx { nonce, max_fee, priority_fee, tx_hash }`. The
nonce and fees are written *before* the send, the hash immediately after it, so a crash at
any point still leaves the next run able to look the transaction up instead of sending
over it. The record is kept for `AwaitingFinality` and cleared only on a terminal outcome
(durable success, or a revert that consumed the nonce). Task invalidation and task removal
both leave it alone.

**Each cycle, for a record that carries a hash:**

| Chain's answer | Outcome |
|----------------|---------|
| receipt, succeeded, durable | clear the record, `Ok(())` - task retires |
| receipt, succeeded, not durable | keep the record, `Err(AwaitingFinality)` - task waits |
| receipt, reverted | clear the record, normal revert error - the task's post-revert event checks run |
| no receipt (never mined, or reorged out) | keep the record and re-send at the **same** nonce, fee-bumped |
| RPC error, missing block number, or a failed durability read | treated as not durable - wait |

The last row is the direction that matters: an endpoint that will not answer is not
evidence that a transaction is absent or final. Waiting another cycle is recoverable;
re-sending over a mined write (a second deposit) or retiring a task whose write vanished
is not.

**`is_l2_block_finalized` (`src/finality.rs`):** the L2 bar, used for `send_snapshot`.
Takes the receipt's *own* L2 block, resolves the batch containing it via
`NodeInterface.findBatchContainingBlock`, finds the matching
`SequencerInbox.SequencerBatchDelivered` on L1 by paginated log scan, and compares that L1
block against L1's `finalized` tag - the same method `is_epoch_finalized` uses, sharing its
tail. It exists separately because "the epoch is finalized" is not the statement we need:
a transaction sent after epoch end sits in a later L2 block and therefore a later batch,
which may not have been posted to L1 at all when the epoch-end batch already has. Gating on
`is_epoch_finalized` would report durable while the write itself was still only
sequencer-promised.

The L1 log scan starts one hour (`BATCH_SCAN_SKEW_SECS`) *before* the L2 block's own
timestamp. Arbitrum derives L2 timestamps from the sequencer's view of L1 time and lets
them run ahead of it, so the raw timestamp can resolve to an L1 block after the batch was
posted, and a forward-only scan started there would walk past the event and report "not
finalized" permanently. An hour is well clear of the protocol's future-time bound and costs
at most ~300 L1 blocks, a fraction of the first 2000-block page.

Like `is_epoch_finalized`, it returns `Ok(true)` immediately when `sequencer_inbox` is
`None` - that is how the Anvil devnet, which has no rollup, runs; `startup.rs` panics if it
is unset in production. Every other unknown ("the node does not have that block yet", "no
batch event within the scan cap") is reported as *not* finalized, so the caller waits.

**Not covered:** a *third party's* challenge that is reorged out after we indexed it - we
would keep a claim record naming a challenger the chain no longer has, and the claim-hash
invariant turns that into a reverted transaction rather than a wrong verdict. A `Verified`
that is reorged out is likewise out of scope: that event is only accepted by the indexer
once it is more than 20 minutes old.

**Starting mid-bridge:** The validator can be started at any time. ## SnapshotSent Filtering

The indexer only processes `SnapshotSent` events from transactions it sent itself (checked via `tx.signer == wallet_address`).

**Why?** `sendSnapshot()` is cheap to call with arbitrary data. An attacker could spam bogus snapshots with invalid `Claim` parameters. If we processed all `SnapshotSent` events, we'd waste gas relaying L2→L1 messages that would revert on Arbitrum's outbox (wrong proof/claim data).

**How it works:** When the validator sees a `Challenged` event, it calls `sendSnapshot` itself. By only indexing our own `SnapshotSent` events, we guarantee we're relaying messages we know are correct.

**Alternative approach (not implemented):** Parse the `L2ToL1Tx` calldata, compare the embedded `Claim` against our `ClaimStore`, verify no prior `SnapshotSent` exists for that epoch, then schedule the relay. This would let us piggyback on other validators' snapshots but adds complexity. The `isSpent` check in `execute_relay` would then serve as the final guard against duplicate relays. For v1, self-filtering is simpler and sufficient.

## L2 Finality Verification

Before executing critical tasks (`validate_claim`, `claim`, `challenge`), the validator verifies the epoch's L2 data is finalized on L1. This prevents acting on data that could theoretically be reorged.

**How it works:**
1. Convert epoch → end timestamp: `(epoch + 1) * epoch_period`
2. Binary search to find the L2 block at that timestamp
3. Query `NodeInterface.findBatchContainingBlock(l2_block)` on Arbitrum to get the batch number
4. Search for `SequencerInbox.SequencerBatchDelivered(batchNum)` event on L1 to find which L1 block contains the batch
5. Compare that L1 block against `eth_getBlockByNumber("finalized")` - if finalized block >= batch block, the epoch is finalized

**Batch event query strategy:** Batches are posted to L1 after L2 transactions, but timing varies significantly - mainnet posts every ~1-3 minutes, while testnet can have gaps of hours or days. To find the `SequencerBatchDelivered` event reliably:
1. Binary search L1 to find the block at `epoch_end_ts` (batch must be posted after the L2 block exists)
2. Paginate forward in 2000-block chunks (~6.6 hours each) until we find the event or reach L1's latest block
3. If not found after scanning to latest, return "not finalized" and reschedule the task for +30 minutes

This approach handles arbitrary batch posting delays without hitting RPC block range limits. If the paginated search becomes too slow in production, we'll switch to indexing `SequencerBatchDelivered` events.

**Configuration:**
- `SEQUENCER_INBOX`: Address of Arbitrum's SequencerInbox on Ethereum L1. **Required in production** - `startup.rs` panics if not set.
- For tests (local Anvil chains), `SEQUENCER_INBOX` is not set. When `sequencer_inbox` is `None`, finality checks return `Ok(true)` immediately, bypassing the check.

**Why finality matters:**
- The 20-minute buffer after epoch end is a heuristic, not a guarantee
- Real finality depends on batch posting to L1 and L1 block finalization (~15-20 min on mainnet)
- Without finality checks, a validator could challenge a valid claim if L2 data reorged after they read it

**Task behavior when not finalized:**
- `ValidateClaim` returns `Err("EpochNotFinalized")` and gets rescheduled +30 minutes.
  The finality check and the snapshot read live together in
  `validate_claim::finalized_state_root`, which is the single entry point for any verdict.
- `Claim` (epoch watcher): returns `Err("EpochNotFinalized")`, retries after 5 minutes. If someone else claims in the meantime, the "Already claimed" check in `claim::execute` detects it and stops.
- This is expected during normal operation when tasks are scheduled close to epoch boundaries, or on testnet where batch posting is sporadic

Git Safety Protocol:
- NEVER update the git config
- NEVER run destructive git commands (push --force, reset --hard, checkout ., restore ., clean -f, branch -D) unless the user explicitly requests these actions. Taking unauthorized destructive actions is unhelpful and can result in lost work, so it's best to ONLY run these commands when given direct instructions 
- NEVER skip hooks (--no-verify, --no-gpg-sign, etc) unless the user explicitly requests it
- NEVER run force push to main/master, warn the user if they request it
- CRITICAL: Always create NEW commits rather than amending, unless the user explicitly requests a git amend. When a pre-commit hook fails, the commit did NOT happen — so --amend would modify the PREVIOUS commit, which may result in destroying work or losing previous changes. Instead, after hook failure, fix the issue, re-stage, and create a NEW commit
- When staging files, prefer adding specific files by name rather than using "git add -A" or "git add .", which can accidentally include sensitive files (.env, credentials) or large binaries
- NEVER commit changes unless the user explicitly asks you to. It is VERY IMPORTANT to only commit when explicitly asked, otherwise the user will feel that you are being too proactive

1. Run the following bash commands in parallel, each using the Bash tool:
  - Run a git status command to see all untracked files. IMPORTANT: Never use the -uall flag as it can cause memory issues on large repos.
  - Run a git diff command to see both staged and unstaged changes that will be committed.
  - Run a git log command to see recent commit messages, so that you can follow this repository's commit message style.
2. Analyze all staged changes (both previously staged and newly added) and draft a commit message:
  - Summarize the nature of the changes (eg. new feature, enhancement to an existing feature, bug fix, refactoring, test, docs, etc.). Ensure the message accurately reflects the changes and their purpose (i.e. "add" means a wholly new feature, "update" means an enhancement to an existing feature, "fix" means a bug fix, etc.).
  - Do not commit files that likely contain secrets (.env, credentials.json, etc). Warn the user if they specifically request to commit those files
  - Draft a concise (1-2 sentences) commit message that focuses on the "why" rather than the "what"
  - Ensure it accurately reflects the changes and their purpose
3. Run the following commands in parallel:
   - Add relevant untracked files to the staging area.
   - Create the commit with a message, ending with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'

   EOF

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

pattern.description: The regular expression pattern to search for in file contents

path.description: File or directory to search in (rg PATH). Defaults to current working directory.

glob.description: Glob pattern to filter files (e.g. "*.js", "*.{ts,tsx}") - maps to rg --glob

output_mode.description: Output mode: "content" shows matching lines (supports -A/-B/-C context, -n line numbers, head_limit), "files_with_matches" shows file paths (supports head_limit), "count" shows match counts (supports head_limit). Defaults to "files_with_matches".

-B.description: Number of lines to show before each match (rg -B). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-A.description: Number of lines to show after each match (rg -A). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (rg -C). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise.

-n.description: Show line numbers in output (rg -n). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to true.

-o.description: Print only the matched (non-empty) parts of each matching line, one match per output line (rg -o / --only-matching). Requires output_mode: "content", ignored otherwise. Defaults to false.

type.description: File type to search (rg --type). Common types: js, py, rust, go, java, etc. More efficient than include for standard file types.

head_limit.description: Limit output to first N lines/entries, equivalent to "| head -N". Works across all output modes: content (limits output lines), files_with_matches (limits file paths), count (limits count entries). Defaults to 250 when unspecified. Pass 0 for unlimited (use sparingly — large result sets waste context).

offset.description: Skip first N lines/entries before applying head_limit, equivalent to "| tail -n +N | head -N". Works across all output modes. Defaults to 0.

multiline.description: Enable multiline mode where . matches newlines and patterns can span lines (rg -U --multiline-dotall). Default: false.

Reads a file from the local filesystem. You can access any file directly by using this tool.
Assume this tool is able to read all files on the machine. If the User provides a path to a file assume that path is valid. It is okay to read a file that does not exist; an error will be returned.

Usage:
- The file_path parameter must be an absolute path, not a relative path
- By default, it reads up to 2000 lines starting from the beginning of the file
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- This tool allows Claude Code to read images (eg PNG, JPG, etc). When reading an image file the contents are presented visually as Claude Code is a multimodal LLM.
- This tool can read PDF files (.pdf). For large PDFs (more than 10 pages), you MUST provide the pages parameter to read specific page ranges (e.g., pages: "1-5"). Reading a large PDF without the pages parameter will fail. Maximum 20 pages per request.

- This tool can only read files, not directories. To list files in a directory, use the registered shell tool.
- You will regularly be asked to read screenshots. If the user provides a path to a screenshot, ALWAYS use this tool to view the file at the path. This tool will work with all temporary file paths.
- If you read a file that exists but has empty contents you will receive a system reminder warning in place of file contents.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time.     is already on chain; a missing receipt is the only path back to fee-bump/re-send.
    An unreadable nonce or an unanswered `finalized` tag waits, never assumes durable.
    
    Remove the now-redundant watchdog: TaskKind::ReconcileClaim, its scheduling and
    invalidation, src/tasks/reconcile_claim.rs, and tests/reconcile_test.rs. Remove
    the hashClaim ABI added with it and recompute the 85-byte preimage in
